recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | Tiko Creator Commerce Expansion + Private Beta Validation
recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @DWSQUIRES，
感谢你这段时间以来的耐心沟通和持续迭代。
自 5 月 6 日收到你的初始提案以来，委员会经历了多轮内部审核，你也在 6 月 6 日根据反馈提交了范围澄清更新。我们对你的响应速度和迭代意愿表示认可——这本身就是 builder 精神的一种体现。但经过对更新版本的仔细审阅，委员会仍然难以形成对项目的清晰判断，本次申请决定为 Rejection。
以下是委员会做出这一决定的完整思考，供你参考：
1. 提案内容经过多轮修订后仍然混乱
你在最新更新中添加了 scope clarification 部分，涵盖了核心假设、交付边界、通过/失败标准、beta 参与者来源、指标和学习报告格式。这些元素的加入方向是正确的，但它们的组织方式使得阅读者难以顺利理解"你到底要做什么、做到什么程度、以及如何验证"。诸多同级序号和它们奇怪的排序导致委员会的评审过程时常中断。
具体而言，比如你增加了预算与工作的映射，但每一周的任务描述仍然是功能清单式的，而你的项目目标是验证业务假设，这显然是不合理的。
2. 委员会的核心疑惑始终未能得到解答
从第一轮审核到最新版本，委员会一直在问同一个问题：你在 Spark 期间具体要验证什么假设？
如果是"创作者是否愿意为数字商品使用 CKB 支付"，那你的 ticketing 基础已经证明了这一点——为什么还要再验证一次？
如果是"Spore 协议适合会员和收藏品场景"，那需要说明 ticketing 场景中什么证据让你相信这个假设可以外推。
如果是"创作者商务平台在 CKB 上有 PMF"，那 beta 的样本量、筛选标准和成功指标是什么？
更新版本中提到了"核心假设"，但这些假设与 ticketing 已验证的内容之间的逻辑关系并未明确。委员会看到的是一份功能开发计划，而非一份假设验证计划。
3. 最终交付成果的质量难以判断
你在 6 月 6 日的更新中提到"The proposal is now narrowed around three reviewable product capabilities and a reproducible beta validation plan"，但委员会仍然无法确认以下问题：
如果 beta 运行 6 周，你将如何定义"成功"？（用户数量？交易笔数？NPS？创作者留存率？）
如果某类能力（如 Memberships）在 beta 中表现不佳，你会如何决定继续、调整还是放弃？
你最终将发布的"学习报告"会包含什么具体数据？委员会如何从这些数据中判断项目是否值得继续资助？
在这些问题没有明确答案的情况下，委员会无法给出负责任的资助承诺。
提案方向值得肯定
以上所有问题都不是方向性的。委员会一致认可你在 ticketing 领域已经取得的成果——一个基于 CKB testnet 的完整活动商务流程（listing → checkout → payment → ticket issuance → QR access → operator check-in → Spore ownership）本身就是对 CKB 创作者经济潜力的有力证明。你也展示了扎实的执行能力和对 Spore 协议的深入理解。
这个方向是对的。CKB 的 Spore 协议在数字商品所有权证明方面确实有独特优势，而创作者商务是一个真实的应用场景。委员会欢迎你打磨之后重新提案。
重新提案的建议
如果你决定继续，委员会建议你从以下几个方面重新思考：
用假设验证式语言重写 To-Do List。每一周的任务应该是"验证 XX 假设"而非"构建 XX 功能"。例如：“Week 1: 验证 5 位目标创作者是否理解 digital drop 的价值主张并愿意预付 → 交付：5 次访谈记录 + 价值主张迭代” 优于 “Week 1: 构建 digital drop creation flow”。
包含你 ticketing 基础的数据。你已经有了一个可测试的产品——用数据说明它的使用情况（测试交易量、用户反馈、遇到的问题），这些数据是委员会判断你执行能力的最佳证据。
重新提案时无需再次提交 ticketing 基础部分的详细描述，重点放在你新增要验证的假设、对应的验证方法和成功标准上。以及按照 Spark Program Mini-Grant 模板 重新组织章节，保证提案内容的排列是逻辑通顺的状态。
再次感谢你的时间和耐心。期待看到你的下一份提案。
Best regards,
Xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee
cc: @zz_tovarishch, @yixiu.ckbfans.bit, @Hanssen

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | CKB-UGMP —— A Universal Spore/DOB Seamless Minting Infrastructure Prototype on CKB —— 基于 CKB 的通用 Spore/DOB 无感铸造基础设施原型
recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @HNO3Miracle，
身体优先，先养好伤。骨折恢复急不得，项目进度慢一点完全没关系，你的健康才是最重要的。周报什么的不用有压力，能跟上就跟上，需要延期的话随时和我说。
关于你在 Mac 平台上达成的 MVP，委员会已经体验过了。目前的效果已经很好，使用体验非常流畅！
另外有一个委员会比较看重的事情希望能得到你的配合：因为 CKB 原有的设计里没有针对 IPFS 的支持做出专门的优化，所以你的实现方式可能成为原有方式的标准补充——也就是说，你的方案不仅对这个项目有价值，对整个 CKB 生态的存储方案都可能是一个重要参考。所以我们希望你能够将目前的实现方式落实为文档，包括：
你是如何通过 Pinata API 将资源上传至 IPFS 的
生成的 CID 是如何写入 Spore DOB 的 dob_metadata 中的
各存储选项（IPFS / 纯文本上链 / 中心化平台）的取舍逻辑
还有一个小问题想请你也在文档中说明一下：为什么有的 DOB 可以看到图片，有的不行？ 我们注意到展示效果有不一致的情况，因此想了解一下是存储方式不同导致的，还是渲染层面的问题。
关于其他平台 JoyID 签名的问题——如果这确实超出了你作为项目开发者的能力范围，不用硬扛。可以在结项报告中如实说明，把已完成的 Mac 平台作为核心交付物，其他平台的兼容性作为已知限制和后续方向即可。
再次提醒，好好休息，身体第一。项目的事不急，等你有精力的时候再慢慢推进。
祝早日康复，
行天
代表 Spark Program 委员会

topics.title: Chiral - Symmetric isomorphic binding: a committee-free, anchor-agnostic protocol where each chain verifies the other with a succinct on-chain light client

recent_posts.topic_title: Chiral - Symmetric isomorphic binding: a committee-free, anchor-agnostic protocol where each chain verifies the other with a succinct on-chain light client
recent_posts.author: janx
recent_posts.content_text:
Excellent work! Great to see the RGB++ idea expanding!
One question I have is that the definition of “leap” here seems to differ from RGB++’s use of the term:
RGB++ leap refers to setting a CKB bound cell’s lock to a seal on any chain other than Bitcoin, e.g. setting the cell’s lock to a CKB or Litecoin seal. ‘Leap’ means transferring an RGB++ asset’s ownership from a Bitcoin seal to a non-Bitcoin one or vice versa. This transfer of ownership between seals on different chains allows RGB++ assets to effectively ‘move across chains without a bridge’.
In Chiral, as described here, ‘leap-in’ looks more like RGB++ ‘mint’ - it creates a new bound cell on CKB and assigns its ownership to a Cardano seal. ‘Leap-out’ seems similar to RGB++’s ‘destroy/burn’. Does it mean that, in Chiral’s leap-in/transfer/leap-out, ownership never transfers to CKB but always remains on Cardano?
Refs
T_Silva:
Leap-in (Cardano → CKB). Alice mints a unique seal NFT at the Plutus binding lock on Cardano, committing to a genesis state S0 (say, “1000 units, royalty = 2%”). A relayer presents that Cardano transaction, plus a Mithril proof that it is certified, to the CKB BoundAsset script, which mints the bound cell carrying S0 and naming Alice’s seal. The asset now lives as programmable state on CKB; ownership stays on Cardano.
T_Silva:
Leap-out (CKB → Cardano). Bob spends the seal on Cardano to a plain output without recreating it. The CKB bound cell is then finalized and burned, its script accepting a proof of the seal’s consumption-without-recreation.
RGB++ leap
Imagine such a situation: what if the unlocking condition of an eUTXO is set to another chain’s UTXO being spent, say, Litecoin’s UTXO? This would mean the ownership of the asset is tied to the Litecoin chain instead, and it should be considered a Litecoin chain asset. The asset magically leaps from the Bitcoin chain to the Litecoin chain — it is “bridged” across chains without a bridge!
Therefore, in the example mentioned above, if Alice wants to transfer her 40 TEST tokens (a Bitcoin Layer 1 asset) to the Litecoin chain, she first needs to spend the corresponding Bitcoin UTXO. Then, a transaction should be constructed on the RGB++ Layer to change the unlocking condition of the eUTXO (containing the asset definition) to her Litecoin UTXO. In this way, the leap from the Bitcoin chain to the Litecoin chain is successful because the ownership (UTXO as unlocking condition) is transferred across chains.
The Bitcoin chain and Litecoin chain in this example can be replaced with any two UTXO-based chains. Such cross-chain leaps are elegant and straightforward, something that only the UTXO model can achieve.
P.S. I couldn’t find any mention of “leap” in the RGB++ light paper or documentation, except for the Medium post. That might be one reason developers interested in RGB++ are getting confused.

recent_posts.topic_title: Chiral - Symmetric isomorphic binding: a committee-free, anchor-agnostic protocol where each chain verifies the other with a succinct on-chain light client
recent_posts.author: phroi
recent_posts.content_text:
For reference, some discussion happened in Nervos Nation in Telegram:
Each chain keeps a small on-chain light client of the other, advanced as that chain progresses. For any event, a relayer submits a proof that the transaction sits under that verified root, checked in-script. Relayers carry bytes only, they can’t forge. We never ship raw state across, just a single-use-seal commitment that’s anchored in the source chain’s real consensus.
RGB++ on its own binds control, not quantity. We add an explicit amount-binding layer on top.
The locked amount lives inside the committed state, not in a free-floating datum field. The ZK proof binds that commitment to the actual lock on the source chain, and the mint/burn policy on the destination enforces that the represented quantity exactly equals the committed amount, no inflation when you mint in, exact burn on the way back out.
So the CKB side knows the cell is worth 20 ADA because that amount rides in the certified commitment
This feels like what RGB++ should have been all along (if only BTC permitted that)

recent_posts.content_html:
For reference, some discussion happened in Nervos Nation in Telegram:

Each chain keeps a small on-chain light client of the other, advanced as that chain progresses. For any event, a relayer submits a proof that the transaction sits under that verified root, checked in-script. Relayers carry bytes only, they can’t forge. We never ship raw state across, just a single-use-seal commitment that’s anchored in the source chain’s real consensus.

RGB++ on its own binds control, not quantity. We add an explicit amount-binding layer on top.

The locked amount lives inside the committed state, not in a free-floating datum field. The ZK proof binds that commitment to the actual lock on the source chain, and the mint/burn policy on the destination enforces that the represented quantity exactly equals the committed amount, no inflation when you mint in, exact burn on the way back out.

So the CKB side knows the cell is worth 20 ADA because that amount rides in the certified commitment

This feels like what RGB++ should have been all along (if only BTC permitted that)

That said, this design is pretty complex, so I’d like to see more investigation on trust boundaries and failures modes, especially code at hand

Keep up the Great Work @T_Silva!!
Phroi

Pocket Node v1.7.3 released — six security fixes from the Nervos team review
The community team’s security review surfaced a batch of findings against v1.7.x. v1.7.3 closes all six. Sideload from the GitHub release; auto-update will roll out to existing installs over the next few hours.
What changed:
Send screen refuses to broadcast a transaction that would leave less than 61 CKB of change. Previously that residue was silently absorbed as fee.
Backing up a raw-key wallet now requires PIN verification before the key is shown. The key is fully masked until you tap to reveal, and the clipboard is cleared 60 seconds after a copy.
Toggling “Authenticate before sending” off now requires re-entering your PIN.
The in-app updater verifies the signing certificate on the downloaded APK before launching the system installer. Tampered or re-signed APKs are refused at the app layer, on top of Android’s own same-key check.
The release workflow now checks out the verified commit instead of the unqualified tag name. Closes a path where a branch named after a tag could shadow the tag at checkout time.
Wallets created on devices without a screen lock now work in a software-only encryption mode and upgrade to hardware-backed protection automatically the moment you enable a device lock.
Thanks to the Nervos community testing team for the review.
Download: Release v1.7.3 · RaheemJnr/pocket-node · GitHub
Source: GitHub - RaheemJnr/pocket-node: A native Android CKB (Nervos) wallet that runs an embedded light client directly on the device via JNI — full sovereignty, no remote servers. · GitHub

[DIS] Rypto — CKB Content & Advocacy Campaign
Summary
This proposal requests a grant of $4,500 over 4 months to fund a dedicated CKB content and advocacy campaign led by Rypto (@RyptoCrypto), a crypto content creator with 30,000+ organic followers across X, YouTube, LinkedIn and CoinMarketCap.
The campaign will deliver consistent short-form video content, written posts, community engagement, and in-person event representation designed to increase CKB’s visibility, simplify its narrative for new audiences, and drive user onboarding during a critical period of ecosystem development.
Grant Amount Requested: $4,500 (paid monthly at $1,125/month)
Duration: 4 months
CKB Wallet Address: ckb1qzda0cr08m85hc8jlnfp3zer7xulejywt49kt2rr0vthywaa50xwsq2fsjgr5kmk45na89d6956qpngkv05kzrqjr6ffs
Project Introduction
What problem does this solve?
Nervos CKB has some of the most compelling technology in blockchain, from its UTXO-based Cell Model to RGB++ and genuine quantum resistance, but it remains significantly under-represented in broader crypto discourse. The gap between what CKB offers and what the wider market knows about it is one of the biggest bottlenecks to ecosystem growth.
This isn’t a technology problem; it’s a visibility and comprehension problem. CKB’s architecture is complex, and most potential users encounter it through technical documentation rather than accessible content that explains why it matters to them.
Why now?
The post-quantum narrative is accelerating across the industry. Projects are scrambling to position themselves as quantum-resistant, while CKB has had this built in from day one. This is a narrow window where CKB’s technical advantages align directly with mainstream market attention, but only if there are credible voices communicating that message to audiences who aren’t already in the Nervos ecosystem.
Simultaneously, developments around Fiber Network, RGB++ maturation, and growing builder activity mean there is a steady pipeline of newsworthy updates that deserve consistent, professional coverage directed at external audiences.
Team & Roles
Rypto (Lead — Content & Advocacy)
Crypto content creator running the Rypto channel (@RyptoCrypto) across X, YouTube and CoinMarketCap
30,000+ organic followers

All content will be structured around three core pillars:
Simplification & Onboarding — Breaking down CKB’s complex architecture into accessible, engaging content that helps new users understand why CKB matters. This is the primary gap in CKB’s current media presence.
Narrative Positioning — Leveraging timely narratives to position CKB within broader market conversations and attract attention from audiences not yet aware of the ecosystem.
Ecosystem Updates — Covering developments across Fiber Network, RGB++, builder activity, governance, and community milestones to keep the wider crypto audience informed about CKB’s progress.
